note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you are an 81-year-old male here about bladder urgency. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: Doc, I have to run to the bathroom all the time. Maybe ten times a day, and I get up three times at night. Sometimes I leak a little before I get there.
Doctor: How long has this been happening?
Patient: About six months now.
Doctor: Any burning when you pass urine? Any blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, and no blood that I have seen.
Doctor: Any fever or pain in your side?
Patient: No fever, no pain in my side.
Doctor: How is your stream? Do you feel like you empty out fully?
Patient: The stream is fine. I think I empty out okay.
Doctor: Any other health problems or medicines?
Patient: Just high blood pressure. I take lisinopril 10 mg every morning, and that is all.
Doctor: Okay. Your urinalysis today was clean, so there is no infection. The bladder scan showed only 30 mL left after you voided, so you are emptying well. Your belly is soft and not tender, and the prostate exam felt smooth and not very enlarged.
Doctor: This is overactive bladder. I would like to start mirabegron 25 mg once daily, because it is gentler on the memory than the older bladder pills. I also want you to try timed voiding every three hours, cut back on caffeine, and drink less in the evening. Mirabegron can raise blood pressure a little, so we will recheck it when I see you again in six weeks. Call us sooner if you cannot pass urine or you see blood.
Patient: That sounds good, Doctor. Thank you.
summary: An 81-year-old male presented to urology with about six months of urinary urgency, up to ten voids a day, getting up three times at night, and occasional leakage. He denied burning, blood in the urine, fever, and side pain. He has high blood pressure treated with lisinopril. Urinalysis was clean, the bladder scan showed a 30 mL residual, and the prostate felt smooth. He was diagnosed with overactive bladder and started on mirabegron 25 mg once daily with timed voiding, less caffeine, and less evening fluid, with follow-up and a blood pressure recheck in six weeks.

soap.subjective: 81-year-old male with about six months of bladder urgency, voiding about ten times a day, getting up three times at night, and leaking a little before reaching the bathroom. Denies burning, blood in the urine, fever, and pain in his side. Stream is fine and he feels he empties fully. History of high blood pressure on lisinopril 10 mg every morning.
soap.objective: Urinalysis today was clean. Bladder scan showed 30 mL left after voiding. Abdomen soft and not tender. Prostate exam felt smooth and not very enlarged.
soap.assessment: Overactive bladder, with no infection and good bladder emptying.
plan: Start mirabegron 25 mg once daily
Timed voiding every three hours, reduce caffeine, and drink less in the evening
Recheck blood pressure at the next visit because mirabegron can raise it
Follow up in six weeks; call sooner if unable to pass urine or if blood is seen

note:
Orthopedic clinic follow-up dictation. This is a 20-year-old male returning for follow-up of a left distal radius fracture, closed, which he sustained about three weeks ago, correction, four weeks ago, when he fell off a bicycle onto an outstretched hand. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and the patient confirmed through the interpreter that he understood each question. He is right-hand dominant. The injury was initially placed in a sugar-tong splint in the emergency department, and a short arm cast was applied one week later once the swelling went down.

Today he reports that his wrist pain is much better, about 2 out of 10 at rest and 4 out of 10 when he moves his fingers. He also reports mild itching under the cast. He denies numbness or tingling in the fingers, fever, and increasing swelling. He denies elbow or shoulder pain. He has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, along with acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. He was also given tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed in the emergency department, but he says he took only two tablets and did not like how it made him feel. He has no known drug allergies. A 25-hydroxyvitamin D level drawn at the last visit returned at 22 nanograms per milliliter, consistent with vitamin D insufficiency.

Vital signs today are blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 64, and temperature 98.4 Fahrenheit. On examination, the skin at the cast edges is intact with no redness or breakdown. The fingers are warm and pink with capillary refill under 2 seconds. Sensation is intact in the median, ulnar, and radial nerve distributions, and he has full active motion of all fingers. There is mild swelling over the dorsum of the hand and mild tenderness over the distal radius. Radiographs of the left wrist, three views, taken today show maintained alignment of the fracture without displacement and early callus formation.

Impression is a left distal radius fracture, healing well and stable in alignment at four weeks, vitamin D insufficiency, and mild cast-related itching without skin breakdown. For the treatment, continue the short arm cast for two more weeks, with repeat radiographs of the left wrist at the next visit, and then transition to a removable wrist splint with referral to hand therapy. Discontinue the tramadol. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed and ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed with food. Start vitamin D3 2000 units daily. I advised him not to put anything inside the cast to scratch the itch and to keep the cast dry. Return precautions were reviewed through the interpreter, and he should come back sooner for numbness, severe pain, color change of the fingers, or fever. Follow up in two weeks.
summary: A 20-year-old male returned to orthopedics four weeks after a left distal radius fracture from a bicycle fall, with a professional interpreter used for the visit. Pain is much improved and he has mild itching under the cast, with no numbness, tingling, fever, or increasing swelling. Radiographs show maintained alignment with early callus, neurovascular exam is intact, and a vitamin D level was low at 22 nanograms per milliliter. He was diagnosed with a healing left distal radius fracture and vitamin D insufficiency. Tramadol was stopped, vitamin D3 2000 units daily was started, the cast continues for two more weeks with repeat radiographs and hand therapy referral, and follow-up is in two weeks.

note:
Dictation for an outpatient visit in the ear, nose and throat clinic with an eye examination as well. This is a 55-year-old male seen for dizziness. He has limited health literacy, so I spoke in plain language throughout and used teach-back for every instruction.

History. He reports about two weeks of spinning dizziness that happens when he rolls over in bed to the right or tips his head back to look at a high shelf. Each spell lasts less than a minute, about 30 seconds, and then settles on its own, with mild nausea afterward. At first he described it as his head feeling off, but when I asked him to show me with his hands he clarified that the room itself spins. He denies hearing loss, ringing in the ears, ear fullness, ear drainage, headache, double vision, slurred speech, facial droop, weakness, and numbness. He denies chest pain and fainting. He has not had any falls.

Past medical history is notable for HTN, T2DM, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis of the right knee. He first told me he takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, but when I had him read the bottle, correction, it is metformin 500 mg twice daily. He also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and aspirin 81 mg daily, and he has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg twice daily for knee pain. He is allergic to meclizine, which caused hives, so I will not prescribe it or any similar vestibular suppressant.

Blood pressure today is 152/88, heart rate 78, and SpO2 98% on room air. His A1c was 7.4% last month and creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL.

Examination. Otoscopy shows clear ear canals and intact tympanic membranes bilaterally with normal landmarks and no effusion. Tuning fork testing shows Weber midline and Rinne with air conduction greater than bone conduction on both sides. Cranial nerves II through XII are intact, Romberg is negative, finger-to-nose is normal, and gait is steady. Visual acuity is 20/25 in each eye with glasses, pupils are equal and reactive, and extraocular movements are full with no spontaneous nystagmus. Fundoscopic exam shows sharp disc margins bilaterally with no papilledema. Dix-Hallpike testing to the right reproduces vertigo with upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency of a few seconds that fatigues in under 30 seconds. Dix-Hallpike testing to the left is negative. I then performed the Epley maneuver on the right in the office, and repeat Dix-Hallpike testing to the right afterward was negative.

Impression is right posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo with a normal neurologic and eye examination today, and also uncontrolled HTN.

For the dizziness, the Epley maneuver was done today. I demonstrated the home exercise and had him repeat it back to me in his own words, and I gave him a picture sheet. Because of the meclizine allergy, I am not prescribing any vestibular suppressant medication. Fall precautions were reviewed, and he should not climb ladders until the spells stop. No imaging is needed now. I will order an MRI of the brain only if the spells change or other neurologic symptoms appear. For his blood pressure, increase amlodipine from 5 mg daily to 10 mg daily. Stop the over-the-counter ibuprofen because of the blood pressure and diabetes, and start acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain. Order a basic metabolic panel in one week. He is due for a dilated diabetic eye exam, so I referred him to ophthalmology. Return to the ear, nose and throat clinic in two weeks, sooner for weakness, trouble speaking, double vision, or a new severe headache.
summary: A 55-year-old male with HTN, T2DM, and hyperlipidemia and limited health literacy presented with two weeks of brief spinning dizziness when rolling over or looking up, without hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or other neurologic symptoms. He has a documented hives reaction to meclizine. The right Dix-Hallpike test reproduced vertigo with torsional nystagmus, and the neurologic and eye examinations were otherwise normal. He was diagnosed with right posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and treated with an Epley maneuver and teach-back home exercises, without vestibular suppressants. Amlodipine was increased to 10 mg daily, ibuprofen was stopped in favor of acetaminophen, and a basic metabolic panel, ophthalmology referral, and ear, nose and throat follow-up in two weeks were arranged.

note:
Doctor: Hello. I understand your daughter is having ear trouble. She is a 4-year-old female, is that right?
Family member: Yes, that's right. She started pulling at her right ear two days ago, and she woke up crying last night. She feels warm too.
Doctor: Has she had any vomiting or diarrhea?
Family member: No vomiting and no diarrhea. She has had a runny nose for about a week, though.
Doctor: Any fluid draining from the ear? Any cough or rash?
Family member: No drainage, no cough, and no rash.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines? Does she take anything regularly?
Family member: No allergies, and nothing regular.
Doctor: Okay. Her temperature today is 100.9, her heart rate is 112, and she weighs 16 kilograms. Her throat is clear and the left ear looks normal. The right eardrum is red and bulging and it does not move well, and there is no tenderness behind the ear. This is acute otitis media of the right ear.
Family member: Does she need antibiotics?
Doctor: Yes, because she has a fever and a bulging eardrum. I will start amoxicillin 720 mg twice a day for 7 days. For pain or fever you can give ibuprofen 160 mg every 6 hours as needed, with food. Offer plenty of fluids. If she is not better in 48 hours, or if she gets a stiff neck, swelling behind the ear, or keeps vomiting, call us or come back.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 4-year-old female was brought in with two days of right ear pulling, waking up crying, and feeling warm, plus about a week of runny nose. There was no vomiting, diarrhea, ear drainage, cough, or rash. Temperature was 100.9 with a red, bulging, poorly moving right eardrum. She was diagnosed with acute otitis media of the right ear and started on amoxicillin 720 mg twice a day for 7 days, with ibuprofen 160 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever. The family was told to return if she is not better in 48 hours.

soap.subjective: 4-year-old female with two days of pulling at her right ear, waking up crying last night, and feeling warm, plus a runny nose for about a week. No vomiting, diarrhea, ear drainage, cough, or rash. No medicine allergies and no regular medications.
soap.objective: Temperature 100.9, heart rate 112, weight 16 kilograms. Throat clear, left ear normal. Right eardrum red and bulging with poor movement, no tenderness behind the ear.
soap.assessment: Acute otitis media of the right ear.
plan: Start amoxicillin 720 mg twice a day for 7 days
Ibuprofen 160 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever, with food
Offer plenty of fluids
Call or return if not better in 48 hours, or for stiff neck, swelling behind the ear, or persistent vomiting

note:
Dermatology clinic dictation. This is a 76-year-old female seen for evaluation of rough, scaly spots on her face and scalp. She reports the spots have been present for about a year and are slowly increasing in number. A few feel tender when she combs her hair. She denies bleeding, rapid growth, and nonhealing sores.

Past history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, and a basal cell carcinoma of the nose that was removed several years ago. She has had a lot of sun exposure over her lifetime. She has been applying over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream 1 percent to the scalp patches for two months without benefit. Her other medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily.

Blood pressure is 134/78 and heart rate is 70. On skin examination of the face, scalp, ears, and dorsal forearms there are multiple erythematous, scaly macules and papules consistent with actinic keratoses, about five on the forehead, six on the scalp, and two on the dorsal left forearm. The lesion on the left temple, correction, the right temple, is thicker, hyperkeratotic, and tender, about 8 millimeters, and I am concerned about a hypertrophic lesion that needs tissue diagnosis. A full skin check shows no suspicious pigmented lesions, and the scar on the nose is clean without any recurrence. Pathology from a biopsy of the left cheek three months ago showed actinic keratosis without malignancy.

For the treatment, I treated 8 of the actinic keratoses today with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy, two freeze-thaw cycles each, and she tolerated it well. A shave biopsy was performed on the thick lesion of the right temple and sent to pathology. Stop the hydrocortisone cream since it is not helping. Start fluorouracil 5 percent cream, applied to the scalp twice daily for 3 weeks, and I reviewed the expected redness, crusting, and soreness with her. She should use a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher every day and wear a hat outdoors. Continue her other medications unchanged. She will return in 4 weeks to review the pathology result and the response to the cream, and she should have a full skin check every year.
summary: A 76-year-old female presented to dermatology with a year of rough, scaly spots on her face and scalp, a few tender, without bleeding, rapid growth, or nonhealing sores. She has hypertension, hypothyroidism, and a prior basal cell carcinoma of the nose, and over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream did not help. Examination showed multiple actinic keratoses, with a thick tender lesion on the right temple, no suspicious pigmented lesions, and no nasal recurrence. Eight lesions were treated with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy and the thick lesion was biopsied. Hydrocortisone was stopped, fluorouracil 5 percent cream was started for the scalp, and she will return in 4 weeks to review pathology.

soap.subjective: 76-year-old female with about a year of rough, scaly spots on the face and scalp that are slowly increasing, with a few tender when combing her hair. Denies bleeding, rapid growth, and nonhealing sores. History of hypertension, hypothyroidism, and basal cell carcinoma of the nose removed years ago; significant lifetime sun exposure. Used over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream 1 percent on the scalp for two months without benefit. Also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 134/78, heart rate 70. Multiple erythematous, scaly macules and papules of the face, scalp, ears, and dorsal forearms consistent with actinic keratoses (about five on the forehead, six on the scalp, two on the left forearm). Right temple lesion thick, hyperkeratotic, tender, about 8 millimeters. Full skin check without suspicious pigmented lesions; nasal scar clean without recurrence. Prior biopsy of the left cheek three months ago showed actinic keratosis without malignancy.
soap.assessment: Actinic keratoses, including a possible hypertrophic lesion of the right temple needing tissue diagnosis.
plan: Liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to 8 actinic keratoses today
Shave biopsy of the thick right temple lesion sent to pathology
Stop hydrocortisone cream
Start fluorouracil 5 percent cream to the scalp twice daily for 3 weeks; expected redness, crusting, and soreness reviewed
Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 30 or higher and a hat outdoors
Continue other medications unchanged
Return in 4 weeks to review pathology and response; full skin check every year

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. Before we start, I want you to know that we have a professional interpreter on the line with us, and I will pause after each sentence so she can interpret. Is that all right?
Patient: Yes, that is fine.
Doctor: Thank you. I see you are a 30-year-old female here for pelvic pain. Tell me about it.
Patient: The pain in my lower belly has been there for almost two years. It gets very bad before and during my period. Some days I cannot go to work.
Doctor: Is the pain there only with your period, or at other times too?
Patient: Mostly with the period, but now there are many days in the month when it hurts, a dull pain on the left side.
Doctor: Does it hurt with intercourse?
Patient: Yes, deep inside. It hurts so much that we avoid it.
Doctor: Any pain with bowel movements?
Patient: Yes, during my period it hurts a lot to have a bowel movement, and sometimes I feel bloated.
Doctor: Any pain when you urinate, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No pain when I urinate, and no blood in the urine.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or bleeding between periods?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no bleeding between periods. But my periods are very heavy, I change a pad every two hours the first two days.
Doctor: Have you lost weight without trying, or had vomiting?
Patient: No weight loss, no vomiting.
Doctor: What have you tried for the pain?
Patient: I took the birth control pill before, but my doctor stopped it because of my migraines with aura. For the pain I take naproxen, the small 220 pills, one or two when it is bad.
Doctor: Let me check the chart. I see naproxen 500 mg twice a day was prescribed at your last visit.
Patient: Oh, yes, you are right. I take the 500 mg one, twice a day, during my period. The small pills are old ones I had at home.
Doctor: Thank you for clarifying. What other health problems and medicines do you have?
Patient: Migraines with aura, and I take sumatriptan 50 mg when I get one. I have acid reflux, and I take omeprazole 20 mg every morning. I was told I have low iron, and I take ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day. And I have depression, and I take sertraline 50 mg every day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: Good. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 82, and temperature 98.2. Your urine pregnancy test today was negative. Your hemoglobin from last week was 10.9 g/dL and your ferritin was low. The transvaginal ultrasound last week showed a 3 cm left ovarian cyst with ground-glass echoes, which looks like an endometrioma, and your chlamydia and gonorrhea tests were negative. On exam, your abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. On the pelvic exam you have deep tenderness behind the uterus and a tender left adnexa, with no mass that I can feel.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: Together, this is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Because you cannot take estrogen with migraines with aura, please do not restart the combined birth control pill. I am going to start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily, which is a progestin-only pill and is safe with migraine with aura. Keep taking naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food during your period, and keep the omeprazole to protect your stomach. Your mood has been low because of the pain, so I will increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg every day. Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day for the low iron. I am also referring you to pelvic floor physical therapy. If the pain is not better in three months, we will talk about laparoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and treat it. I want to see you back in eight weeks. Go to the emergency room for sudden severe pain, fainting, or fever.
Patient: Okay, thank you, Doctor.
summary: A 30-year-old female seen with a professional interpreter reported almost two years of chronic pelvic pain, worse around her period, with deep pain during intercourse, painful bowel movements, and heavy periods, without urinary symptoms, fever, discharge, or weight loss. Her history includes migraines with aura, acid reflux, low iron, and depression, and her combined birth control pill was stopped for the migraines. Ultrasound showed a 3 cm left ovarian cyst consistent with an endometrioma, and hemoglobin was 10.9 g/dL. She was diagnosed with chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily was started, sertraline was increased to 100 mg every day, and pelvic floor physical therapy and eight-week follow-up were arranged.

soap.subjective: 30-year-old female, interpreter used. Almost two years of lower abdominal pain that is severe before and during her period, now with a dull left-sided pain on many days, deep pain with intercourse, painful bowel movements during her period, bloating, and very heavy periods. Denies pain when urinating, blood in the urine, fever, discharge, bleeding between periods, weight loss, and vomiting. Previously on a combined birth control pill that was stopped because of migraines with aura. Initially reported taking small 220 naproxen pills, then clarified she takes naproxen 500 mg twice a day during her period. Also has migraines with aura on sumatriptan 50 mg, acid reflux on omeprazole 20 mg every morning, low iron on ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day, and depression on sertraline 50 mg every day. No medicine allergies.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 82, temperature 98.2. Urine pregnancy test negative. Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, ferritin low. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 3 cm left ovarian cyst with ground-glass echoes consistent with an endometrioma. Chlamydia and gonorrhea tests negative. Abdomen soft with mild left lower quadrant tenderness. Pelvic exam with deep tenderness behind the uterus and a tender left adnexa, no palpable mass.
soap.assessment: Chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis.
plan: Start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily; do not restart the combined birth control pill because of migraines with aura
Continue naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food during her period and continue omeprazole
Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg every day
Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day
Referral to pelvic floor physical therapy
Discuss laparoscopy if the pain is not better in three months
Follow up in eight weeks; go to the emergency room for sudden severe pain, fainting, or fever

note:
Pediatric hospital medicine progress note, hospital day 2, for a 10-year-old male admitted with an asthma exacerbation. A professional Spanish video interpreter was used for the entire discussion with his mother, and she confirmed understanding using teach-back.

Overnight events: He required nasal cannula oxygen at 1 L/min overnight for low oxygen readings while asleep, and this was weaned off at around 4 in the morning. He had no fever overnight. His albuterol nebulizers were spaced from every 2 hours to every 3 hours overnight. This morning his mother reports that his cough is less frequent and that he slept most of the night. He denies chest pain, abdominal pain, and vomiting.

Current medications: albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 3 hours, prednisone 40 mg by mouth once daily (day 2 of 5), and his home fluticasone 110 mcg, two puffs twice daily, which was continued from admission.

Vitals this morning: temperature 98.9 F, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 24, blood pressure 104/62, and SpO2 95% on room air. He has been off oxygen for about 6 hours.

Exam: He is sitting up, alert, and speaking in full sentences. There are no retractions. Breath sounds show mild end-expiratory wheezes in both lower lung fields with good air movement and a mildly prolonged expiratory phase. Heart sounds are regular without murmur. Abdomen is soft.

Data: The admission chest x-ray showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. A respiratory viral panel was negative.

Asthma exacerbation, improving: He is clinically better and no longer needs oxygen. Continue prednisone 40 mg once daily to complete 5 days. Space albuterol to every 4 hours today, and if he tolerates this for 12 hours with SpO2 above 92% on room air, anticipate discharge tomorrow. Continue fluticasone 110 mcg, two puffs twice daily. Asthma education was done with the interpreter, including spacer technique, trigger avoidance, and a written asthma action plan in Spanish.

Disposition: Regular diet. Follow up with his pediatrician within 3 days of discharge.
summary: A 10-year-old male was hospitalized with an asthma exacerbation, and a professional Spanish interpreter was used for his mother on hospital day 2. He needed low-flow oxygen overnight, was weaned to room air with SpO2 95%, and had no fever, chest pain, abdominal pain, or vomiting. Exam showed mild end-expiratory wheezes without retractions, the chest x-ray showed hyperinflation without consolidation, and a viral panel was negative. Asthma exacerbation is improving on prednisone 40 mg once daily and albuterol, which is being spaced to every 4 hours, with home fluticasone continued. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow with asthma education and pediatrician follow-up within 3 days.

Sitting up, alert, speaking in full sentences, no retractions. Mild end-expiratory wheezes in both lower lung fields with good air movement and mildly prolonged expiratory phase. Heart sounds regular without murmur. Abdomen soft. Admission chest x-ray showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Respiratory viral panel negative.

Space albuterol to every 4 hours today; if tolerated for 12 hours with SpO2 above 92% on room air, anticipate discharge tomorrow
Continue fluticasone 110 mcg, two puffs twice daily
Asthma education with the interpreter, including spacer technique, trigger avoidance, and a written asthma action plan in Spanish
Regular diet
Follow up with his pediatrician within 3 days of discharge

note:
40-year-old female, urgent care visit.

Visit modality: Audio-only telephone visit. The patient was at home and gave verbal consent to a phone visit. No video was available, so no visual examination could be performed.

Reason for visit: Recurrent tonsillitis. This is a 26-year-old female with another sore throat for 4 days. She is currently about 14 weeks pregnant.

History: She reports 4 days of sore throat, pain with swallowing, and fever. She also reports tender swollen glands in her neck and a hoarse voice. This is her fourth episode of tonsillitis in the past 12 months, and each earlier episode was treated with antibiotics. Her partner looked at her throat with a flashlight and saw white patches on both tonsils. She denies difficulty breathing, drooling, trouble opening her mouth, a muffled voice, neck stiffness, rash, cough, vaginal bleeding, and abdominal cramping. She had a rapid strep test at our lab yesterday morning, which was positive, and a CBC showed WBC 13.2.

Past medical history: asthma, hypothyroidism, and GERD. She has no known drug allergies. She first told me she takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, but after reading the bottle she corrected this, and the dose is 75 mcg daily. She also uses albuterol as needed for asthma, famotidine 20 mg twice daily for GERD, a prenatal vitamin daily, and over-the-counter ibuprofen as needed for throat pain. Her TSH last week was 4.6 mIU/L.

Patient-reported measurements: Temperature 101.3 F this morning on her home thermometer. Home cuff blood pressure 112/70 and heart rate 96. SpO2 98% on a home finger pulse oximeter.

Observations by phone: She speaks in full sentences with a mildly hoarse voice. I could not hear stridor or a muffled voice.

Impression: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis with recurrent tonsillitis in a patient who is 14 weeks pregnant. Hypothyroidism with a TSH above the target for pregnancy.

Recommendations: Start penicillin V potassium 500 mg twice daily for 10 days, which is compatible with pregnancy. Take acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for throat pain and fever. Stop the ibuprofen, because NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy. I also advised against tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics in pregnancy. Increase levothyroxine from 75 mcg to 88 mcg daily, with a repeat TSH in 4 weeks. Continue albuterol as needed, famotidine 20 mg twice daily, and the prenatal vitamin daily. Use warm salt-water gargles and drink plenty of fluids. I will notify her obstetrician about the infection and the thyroid dose change. Given four episodes in a year, I am referring her to ENT to discuss tonsillectomy after delivery. She should go to the emergency department for difficulty breathing, drooling, inability to swallow fluids, or trouble opening her mouth. I will call her in 3 days to check on her response to the antibiotic.

A rapid strep test was positive and WBC was 13.2, and she has asthma, hypothyroidism, and GERD with a TSH of 4.6. note:
Dermatology clinic dictation. This is a 20-year-old female with a long history of atopic dermatitis who presents with a flare over the past 6 weeks that has not responded to her usual topical therapy. She reports intense itching, worse at night, that wakes her 3 to 4 nights a week, and red patches in the antecubital and popliteal folds, the neck, and around both eyes. For the past 3 days she has noticed oozing and honey-colored crusts on the left antecubital fossa. She denies fever, eye pain, vision changes, and joint pain. She also denies any new soaps, detergents, or pets.

Past medical history includes asthma and allergic rhinitis. She is allergic to penicillin, which caused hives as a child, so penicillin-class antibiotics are to be avoided. Medications as she describes them are triamcinolone 0.1 percent cream, which she says she applies twice daily, correction, once daily at night, to the arms, legs, and underarms for several weeks, tacrolimus 0.1 percent ointment twice daily to the face and neck, cetirizine 10 mg daily, fluticasone inhaler 110 mcg two puffs twice daily, and albuterol as needed.

On examination there is diffuse dryness with lichenified, excoriated, erythematous plaques in both antecubital and popliteal fossae, the posterior neck, and the eyelids, with periorbital hyperpigmentation. The left antecubital fossa has a 4 centimeter weeping patch with honey-colored crust consistent with secondary impetiginization. There is skin thinning with early striae in both axillary folds where the triamcinolone has been applied. No vesicles or punched-out erosions to suggest eczema herpeticum. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Her EASI score is 24. Labs from last week show total IgE 640 IU/mL and eosinophils 7 percent, with a CBC otherwise normal. A bacterial swab of the crusted area was sent today.

Impression is moderate to severe atopic dermatitis flare with secondary bacterial infection of the left antecubital fossa, along with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Topical steroid skin thinning in the axillae.

For the treatment, stop the triamcinolone cream because of the skin thinning. Start mometasone 0.1 percent ointment twice daily to the body for 2 weeks, then twice weekly for maintenance. Continue tacrolimus 0.1 percent ointment twice daily to the face, neck, and eyelids. Start mupirocin 2 percent ointment three times daily for 7 days to the crusted area. Because of the penicillin allergy, if an oral antibiotic is needed after the swab result I will use doxycycline and not a penicillin-class drug. Increase cetirizine from 10 mg daily to 10 mg twice daily to help with night itching. Given the moderate to severe disease, I discussed dupilumab and we will start dupilumab 600 mg loading dose and then 300 mg every 2 weeks once the prior authorization is approved, with teaching on injections and the risk of conjunctivitis. Continue the fluticasone inhaler and albuterol per her primary care provider. She should use a fragrance-free emollient twice daily and dilute bleach baths twice weekly. Follow up in 4 weeks, sooner for fever, painful blistering rash, or eye symptoms.

She has a penicillin allergy (childhood hives) and skin thinning with early striae in the axillae from triamcinolone. Her EASI score was 24 and a bacterial swab was sent. She was diagnosed with a moderate to severe atopic dermatitis flare with secondary bacterial infection. Triamcinolone was stopped, mometasone and mupirocin were started, cetirizine was increased, and dupilumab was planned pending authorization, with follow-up in 4 weeks.

She has had irregular periods since age 15, with cycles every 40 to 60 days, along with acne and coarse hair growth on her chin. She denies galactorrhea, headaches, and heat intolerance. She takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies.

Her blood pressure is 118/74, heart rate 72, and BMI is 31. Fasting glucose is 92, hemoglobin A1c is 5.4%, TSH is 2.1, and prolactin is normal. Total testosterone is elevated at 62 ng/dL. A pelvic ultrasound shows polycystic-appearing ovaries with about 12 follicles in each ovary. A urine pregnancy test today is negative.

Impression is polycystic ovary syndrome with oligomenorrhea, acne, and hirsutism, without diabetes or thyroid disease.

For the plan, start metformin 500 mg once daily with dinner, and increase to 500 mg twice daily after 2 weeks if she tolerates it. Start a combined oral contraceptive pill, one tablet daily, to regulate her periods and improve the acne and hair growth. I counseled her on a healthy diet, regular exercise, and a goal of losing 5 to 10 percent of her body weight. Follow up in 3 months with a repeat hemoglobin A1c.

note:
Visit modality: Telehealth video visit for neurology follow-up after an emergency department evaluation. The patient is a 72-year-old female who joined from home by video with her husband present, who witnessed the event. Identity and location were confirmed, and the patient consented to the visit.

Reason for visit: First unprovoked seizure.

History: Five days ago she had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home that lasted about 2 minutes by her husband's account, with a bitten tongue and urinary incontinence, followed by about 30 minutes of confusion. The patient first said the event was 3 days ago, but her husband corrected this, and it was 5 days ago. She had no warning symptoms and has never had a seizure before. She denies fever, headache, neck stiffness, head injury, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, new weakness, and speech difficulty. She returned 2 weeks ago from a 3-week trip to rural India, where she ate street food, including pork dishes.

In the emergency department, a noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute bleed or mass and mild chronic small vessel changes. Labs showed sodium 138, glucose 118, creatinine 1.2 with an eGFR of 46, and WBC 8.4. The ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate. She was started on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily and discharged.

Past medical history: HTN, T2DM, atrial fibrillation, hypothyroidism, and chronic low back pain. Medications: apixaban 5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tramadol 50 mg every 8 hours as needed for back pain, and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily since the emergency department visit. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: blood pressure 138/80, heart rate 74, and temperature 98.2 F.

Limited video examination: She is alert and fully oriented, with fluent speech and no dysarthria. Her face is symmetric. There is no arm drift on 10-second arm extension, and finger-to-nose is normal on both sides. A small healing laceration is visible on the right lateral tongue. Gait was not assessed.

Impression: First unprovoked seizure in a 72-year-old, which is new-onset late-life epilepsy until proven otherwise. A structural cause such as stroke or tumor, a metabolic cause, and an infectious cause such as neurocysticercosis after her recent travel to an endemic area are all being considered. Tramadol may lower her seizure threshold. She also takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, so levetiracetam is a good choice because it does not interact with apixaban.

Recommendations: Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. Stop the tramadol and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain. Decrease metformin from 1000 mg twice daily to 500 mg twice daily because of the eGFR of 46. Order an MRI of the brain with and without contrast, a routine EEG, a repeat BMP and CBC, and cysticercosis serology. Seizure precautions were reviewed: no driving, no bathing alone, and no climbing on heights until cleared. Call 911 for a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. We will have a video follow-up in 2 weeks after the results return, sooner for another seizure, fever, severe headache, or confusion.

She recently returned from rural India and denied fever, headache, neck stiffness, and focal symptoms. She has HTN, T2DM, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, and hypothyroidism, and ED head CT was without acute findings. The impression was new-onset late-life seizure with structural, metabolic, and infectious causes such as neurocysticercosis under consideration. Levetiracetam continues, tramadol was stopped, metformin was reduced, and MRI of the brain, EEG, labs, and cysticercosis serology were ordered with video follow-up in 2 weeks.

Doctor: Hello, thanks for coming in. I see you are a 34-year-old female here to talk about birth control. What are you looking for?
Patient: I have two kids and I am done for now, but I do not want anything permanent. I am using condoms and they are not great.
Doctor: Okay. Do you have any health problems or take any medicines?
Patient: I get migraines with aura, and I take sumatriptan 50 mg when one starts. And my periods are heavy.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Yes, ibuprofen gives me hives, so I cannot take ibuprofen or Advil or anything like it.
Doctor: Good to know, I will make sure nothing like that is prescribed. Do you smoke? Any chest pain, leg swelling, or pelvic pain?
Patient: I do not smoke. No chest pain, no leg swelling, and no pelvic pain. No bleeding between periods either.
Doctor: What about unusual discharge or pain with sex?
Patient: No discharge and no pain with sex.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 112/70. Your urine pregnancy test is negative, and your Pap smear from last year was normal. On the exam, your abdomen is soft, and the uterus is normal in size, mobile, and not tender.
Patient: So what are my options?
Doctor: Because you have migraines with aura, you should not use any method that contains estrogen, so the pill, patch, and ring are out. A hormonal or a copper IUD would both work well for you. The levonorgestrel IUD would also make your heavy periods lighter, so I recommend that one. It lasts for years and is easy to remove if you change your mind.
Patient: Does it hurt to put in?
Doctor: Most people have cramping for a few minutes. Since you cannot take ibuprofen, I will have you take acetaminophen 1000 mg one hour before the insertion. Until the IUD is in, I would like you to start norethindrone 0.35 mg, one pill every day at the same time, as a bridge. It does not contain estrogen, so it is safe with your migraines. Keep using condoms for the first week.
Patient: Okay, that works for me.
Doctor: Keep the sumatriptan for your migraines as you have been. We will schedule the IUD insertion in two weeks, and I will see you for a check four to six weeks after that. Call us if you have heavy bleeding, fever, or severe belly pain after the insertion.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.
summary: A 34-year-old female presented for contraception counseling, wanting a reliable but non-permanent method. She has migraines with aura on sumatriptan and heavy periods, and she is allergic to ibuprofen, which causes hives. She denied chest pain, leg swelling, pelvic pain, bleeding between periods, and discharge, and her blood pressure was 112/70 with a negative urine pregnancy test. Estrogen-containing methods were ruled out because of the migraines with aura, and a levonorgestrel IUD was recommended. Norethindrone 0.35 mg every day was started as a bridge, acetaminophen 1000 mg is planned before insertion because of the NSAID allergy, and IUD insertion is scheduled in two weeks.

Doctor: Good morning, come on in. I see you are a 61-year-old male here about erectile dysfunction. What brings you in today?
Patient: Morning, Doctor. I have a lot of questions, if that's all right. I got back from a trip abroad about two weeks ago, and I've been worried sick. For about eight months I've had trouble getting and keeping an erection. Is that serious? Could it be my heart?
Doctor: Those are good questions, and we will go through them one at a time. First, the history. Do you still get morning erections?
Patient: Less than before. Maybe once a week. Is that a bad sign?
Doctor: It tells me there may be both physical and stress factors. Do you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness when you exert yourself?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath. I do feel a little lightheaded when I stand up fast, though. Is that related? Should I be worried about that?
Doctor: We will come back to that. Any burning with urination, discharge, or sores?
Patient: No burning, no discharge, no sores. But could I have caught something while traveling? I did have one encounter I regret.
Doctor: I hear you, and we will test you for peace of mind. What other health problems do you have, and what do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, and an enlarged prostate. I take lisinopril 20 mg every morning, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, and tamsulosin 0.8 mg at night. No, wait, tamsulosin is 0.4 mg, one capsule. I always mix that up.
Doctor: Okay, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night. Do you use nitroglycerin or any heart medicine like a nitrate?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Is that important?
Doctor: Very important, and I will explain in a moment. Did you take anything else for the erections?
Patient: Yes, I bought some male enhancement pills at a market on the trip. I took one twice. I got a pounding headache and my face was flushed, and I got scared. Were those dangerous? What was in them?
Doctor: Those pills are not regulated, and some contain hidden sildenafil, so I do not want you taking them again. Let me share your numbers. Your BP today is 138/84, your pulse is 76, and your BMI is 29. Your ECG today shows a normal sinus rhythm with no signs of a prior heart attack. Your labs from last week show an A1c of 7.1%, LDL of 128 mg/dL, creatinine of 1.0, total testosterone of 410 ng/dL, and PSA of 1.8. On exam, your genital exam is normal, the testes are normal in size, and the prostate is smooth, mildly enlarged, and not tender. Your IIEF-5 score is 12, which is moderate erectile dysfunction.
Patient: So is it my heart? Is it my hormones? Is it all in my head?
Doctor: Your heart tracing is reassuring, and your testosterone is normal. I think this is erectile dysfunction from a mix of blood vessel risk factors, meaning diabetes, high blood pressure, and cholesterol, plus performance anxiety after the first episodes.
Patient: Will I need surgery? Is the medicine safe? Can I have a glass of wine with it?
Doctor: No surgery. I will start tadalafil 5 mg once daily, which also helps the prostate symptoms. One glass of wine is fine. Never take it with nitrates, and stand up slowly because it can lower your blood pressure, especially together with tamsulosin, so keep taking tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night. Stop the pills from the market. I am also increasing atorvastatin from 20 mg to 40 mg at bedtime because your LDL is high for someone with diabetes. I will order a urine chlamydia and gonorrhea test and HIV and syphilis tests, and I will give you a written summary because you have a lot of questions. I would also like to refer you to a counselor for the anxiety. Please see me in six weeks. Call us for an erection lasting more than four hours, chest pain, or a severe headache.
Patient: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything, Doctor.

He denied chest pain, shortness of breath, burning, discharge, and sores, but reported lightheadedness on standing and headache and flushing after unregulated enhancement pills bought abroad. He has high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, and an enlarged prostate; ECG, testosterone, and PSA were reassuring, with A1c 7.1% and LDL 128 mg/dL. The diagnosis was erectile dysfunction from vascular risk factors plus performance anxiety. Tadalafil 5 mg daily was started, the market pills were stopped, atorvastatin was increased to 40 mg, and STI testing, counseling referral, and six-week follow-up were arranged.

Inpatient ophthalmology follow-up dictation on the hospital ward. This is a 50-year-old male with primary open-angle glaucoma whom I am seeing at the bedside during his admission for right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia, hospital day 3. I was asked to see him because his home eye drops were not on his medication reconciliation.

He reports that he stopped both of his glaucoma drops about 2 months ago because of cost. They were latanoprost 0.005 percent at bedtime and a brand-name combination of dorzolamide-timolol twice daily, with a copay of about 90 dollars a month. He first said he stopped only the combination drop, correction, he stopped both drops around the same time. He denies eye pain, blurred vision, halos around lights, headache, and nausea. He reports narrowing of his peripheral vision on the left, which he has noticed over the past few months. His right eye, correction, his left eye, is the worse one.

Past medical history is type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, and his home lisinopril 10 mg daily. Temperature is 99.1 F, blood pressure 136/82, heart rate 80, respiratory rate 18, and SpO2 96% on room air. WBC is 11.4, down from 15.2 on admission. The admission chest x-ray showed a right lower lobe infiltrate.

Eye examination: Visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye with correction. Pupils are equal and reactive with no afferent defect. Intraocular pressure by Goldmann applanation tonometry is 24 mmHg in the right eye and 26 mmHg in the left eye, which is above his target pressure of 18 or lower. The corneas are clear, the anterior chambers are deep and quiet, and there is no redness. The cup-to-disc ratio is 0.7 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye with inferior rim thinning. His last visual field 4 months ago showed a superior arcuate defect in the left eye.

Impression is primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes, worse on the left, with elevated pressures due to cost-related nonadherence, community-acquired pneumonia that is improving, and type 2 diabetes.

For the treatment, restart latanoprost 0.005 percent, one drop in both eyes at bedtime, using the low-cost generic. Discontinue the brand-name dorzolamide-timolol combination for now because of the cost. Continue the pneumonia treatment per the primary team. I have asked social work and pharmacy to review medication assistance programs and a 90-day generic supply before discharge. I taught him how to instill the drops. He will follow up in the glaucoma clinic in 2 weeks for a pressure recheck and a repeat visual field, and I will consider laser trabeculoplasty if the pressures stay high.

He denied eye pain, blurred vision, halos, headache, and nausea but reported narrowing of peripheral vision on the left. Intraocular pressures were 24 mmHg right and 26 mmHg left with cup-to-disc ratios of 0.7 and 0.8, and WBC had improved to 11.4. He was diagnosed with bilateral glaucoma with cost-related nonadherence, improving pneumonia, and type 2 diabetes. Generic latanoprost 0.005 percent was restarted at bedtime, the brand dorzolamide-timolol was discontinued, social work and pharmacy will review assistance, and glaucoma clinic follow-up is in 2 weeks.
